title: Victorian summary offences: imprisonment capped at two years
statement: The Magistrates' Court deals with summary offences and indictable offences triable summarily. For Victorian summary offences the maximum term of imprisonment is fixed at two years, regardless of what maximum penalty is specified for the offence. The cap does not raise a lower specified maximum: the offence’s own maximum remains the absolute ceiling (5.1). Summary offences may or may not be punishable by imprisonment, and need care in combination with offences attracting a custodial term.

title: Victorian indictable offences triable summarily; two-year cap per offence; five-year cumulative cap
statement: Victorian indictable offences (statutory and common law) triable summarily include those listed in Schedule 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2009, Level 5 or Level 6 offences, offences punishable by Level 5 or 6 imprisonment or fine, and offences punishable by up to 10 years, a fine of 1200 penalty units, or both. The list is inclusive and Schedule 2 is a separate route (the Manual does not reproduce it). The Magistrates’ Court may not impose more than two years for any single offence, nor a cumulative term over five years for multiple offences committed at the same time unless an Act expressly provides (enforced by mc.two_year_max_summary and cum.magistrates_5_years).

title: When imprisonment is available for the offence
statement: A statutory offence is punishable by imprisonment only if that sanction is expressly provided for, generally by a prescribed maximum penalty. Almost all indictable offences are punishable by imprisonment; possession of a small quantity of cannabis is punishable only by a fine. Where a statutory offence is created but no maximum penalty is specified, the maximum is presumptively two years imprisonment. Common law offences are punishable by imprisonment, with a maximum set by statute or “at large”. Summary offences may or may not be punishable by imprisonment.

title: Minimum non-parole period for standard sentence offences (s 11A(4))
statement: When sentencing for a standard sentence offence within the scheme (sso.scope), or for multiple offences including one, the court must, unless it considers it is not in the interests of justice, fix a non-parole period of at least 30 years for a life term, 70% of the relevant term if it is 20 years or more, and 60% if it is 20 years or less. Reasons must be given for a shorter non-parole period. As printed, a term of exactly 20 years falls in both limbs; and for short terms the floor cannot be met together with the 12-month and six-month restrictions in 8.3.1.
logic: only where a charge passes sso.scope: life -> npp >= 30 years; relevant term > 20 years -> npp >= 70%; relevant term < 20 years -> npp >= 60%; exactly 20 years -> enforce 60% (12 years) as the floor and caution if below 70% (14 years) (flag.sso_npp_20_year_overlap); a lower npp needs stated interests-of-justice reasons. title: The 'usual' non-parole period (60–75%) and reasons for departing
statement: In practice non-parole periods usually fall between 60% and 75% of the head sentence; this is an important guide, but there is "no usual non-parole period", different standards may apply for longer and shorter sentences, and the range ceases to be of much guidance where the head sentence is around 10 years or more. title: Offender already serving a non-parole period: fix a new single non-parole period
statement: If the offender is serving the non-parole period of a prior sentence (the “parole sentence”) and receives a further term, the court must fix a new single non-parole period for all sentences; it supersedes the earlier one and must not make the offender eligible for parole earlier than if the new sentence had not been imposed. It is wrong to approach the new sentence as if there must be an “overall minimum term” made up of the time remaining on the parole sentence and a non-parole period for the new sentence. The requirement does not apply where the prior sentence was originally a straight sentence without parole eligibility, where the original non-parole period has been completed, or to an offender sentenced at one time for offences across multiple indictments. The new single non-parole period is not a “sentence of imprisonment” for the purposes of determining when a sentence commences. Courts are encouraged to commence it from the date of the new sentence (on appeal, the date of the order under appeal); the date must be expressly stated; and where it runs from the new sentence date the court must make an allowance for the parole sentence already served. title: Categories where cumulation is the default
statement: The default is cumulation rather than concurrency for terms of imprisonment for: defaulting on a fine or payment of money (only for uncompleted terms relating to a similar default); a prison offence or escape; a serious offender convicted of a relevant offence; an offence committed while on parole or for breaching parole; an offence committed while on bail; a young offender whose later offending was escape or property damage to specified correctional facilities; the four offences of (aggravated) intentionally or recklessly exposing an emergency worker, custodial officer or youth justice custodial worker to risk by driving; and damaging an emergency vehicle. All remain subject to fundamental principles, in particular totality. For a prison offence, escape, breach of parole or offending on parole, “exceptional circumstances” must be found to displace the prima facie cumulation of new sentences with the previous sentence. For fine or payment defaults, a serious offender convicted of a relevant offence, offending on bail, and specified offences against emergency workers and custodial officers, the court has a wide discretion whether to order concurrency and totality can justify departing from the presumption. title: No cumulation on a life sentence (imposed now, already imposed or being served, or paroled from)

title: Renzella discretion and 'dead time'
statement: Courts have a common law discretion to take into account custody not covered by a s 18 declaration (eg residential rehabilitation or immigration detention), weighted by its burden: it is not equivalent to real incarceration and does not necessarily attract the same deduction. "Dead time" (custody that in hindsight should not have been served) is reflected by reducing the base sentence or moderating cumulation, by the amount the court considers appropriate. Time served under a previous sentence is not declarable PSD; the court must make clear that it took the earlier sentence into account through totality. Previous detention should be taken into account at the earliest opportunity, not left to a later court (though the discretion has been exercised for custody in the distant past). The discretion does not operate where the offender is on parole from a life sentence.

title: Indefinite sentence: availability, threshold and procedure
statement: An adult convicted of a 'serious offence' by the Supreme or County Court may be sentenced to an indefinite term, regardless of the maximum penalty, on the court’s own initiative or the DPP’s application. No non-parole period is fixed; the court fixes a “nominal sentence” equal to the non-parole period of the fixed term it might have imposed. As preventative detention at odds with proportionality, the power is exercised sparingly, in the exceptional case. Before imposing it the court must consider whether the Court Secure Treatment Order provisions apply (if so, it must make that order instead) and be satisfied to a high degree of probability that, at sentencing, the offender is a serious danger to the community (the prosecution bears the burden). In deciding serious danger it must consider: whether the nature of the serious offence is exceptional; anything relevant in the transcript of any proceeding for a serious offence; any medical, psychiatric or other relevant report; the risk of serious danger if no indefinite sentence is imposed and the need to protect the community; and anything else it thinks fit. Procedure: DPP notice (day of conviction or within five working days) and application (within 10 working days); explanation to the offender within five working days of conviction; adjournment of at least 25 working days after conviction; evidence and submissions, victim impact statements and pre-sentence reports considered; reasons given and recorded; any period detained under a Court Assessment Order deducted from the nominal sentence where the psychiatrist’s report was made under it.

title: Indefinite sentence: review, discharge and appeal
statement: An indefinite sentence must be reviewed on the DPP’s application as soon as practicable after the nominal sentence is served, on the offender’s application three years after that review, and then at intervals of not less than three years. Unless satisfied to a high degree of probability that the offender still poses a danger to the community, the reviewing court must discharge the indefinite sentence, make the offender subject to a re-integration program and issue a warrant as if for a five-year term; otherwise the indefinite sentence continues. A review is not “imposing sentence”, so the reviewing court should assume the authorities will responsibly exercise their statutory powers. The offender may appeal a refusal to discharge and the DPP may appeal a discharge.

title: Category 1 offences: imprisonment without a CCO
statement: For most Category 1 offences a court must impose a sentence of imprisonment and must not attach a CCO. title: Category 2 'substantial and compelling, exceptional and rare' test
statement: The Category 2 exceptions closely follow the special-reason test, including the weight given to general deterrence and denunciation, limits on considering good character, plea, rehabilitation or parity, and a need to have regard to Parliament’s intention that imprisonment should ordinarily be imposed for offences of this type. The residual exception is a category of limited scope: a stringent, non-discretionary test, a higher hurdle than Verdins, which the Court of Appeal has said will not often, if ever, be satisfied — though that observation only describes the apparent operation of the legislation, and the difficulty may vary with the offence. Two steps: are there substantial and compelling circumstances (weighty enough to justify no custody), and are they exceptional and rare (wholly outside the run-of-the-mill factors typical of the offending)? General deterrence and denunciation have primacy; personal circumstances get less weight than the gravity of the offending; previous good character, early plea, rehabilitation prospects and even parity must not be considered (the special-reason test instead excepts a lack of previous convictions: flag.good_character_category2_vs_special_reason). It is evaluative: minds may reasonably differ, an accumulation of detail may compel the conclusion, and each case turns on its own facts.

statement: For the manslaughter minimum, gross violence requires proof beyond reasonable doubt that the offender (1) caused the victim’s death in company with two or more people, or entered into an agreement, arrangement or understanding with two or more people to engage in the conduct that caused the death; and (2) planned in advance to have and use an offensive weapon or firearm and did use it to cause the victim’s death, or planned in advance to engage in the conduct that caused the death when at the time of planning a reasonable person would have foreseen it would be likely to result in death, or caused two or more serious injuries to the victim during a sustained or prolonged attack. A single punch or strike requires proof beyond reasonable doubt that the death was caused by a punch or strike taken to be a dangerous act, that the offender intended it to be delivered to the head or neck, that the victim was not expecting it, and that the offender knew the victim was not expecting (or was probably not expecting) it; the unexpected punch or strike must be the one that caused death and was intended (the victim need not expect any punch at all). These elements are given for manslaughter only: for causing serious injury in circumstances of gross violence (9.1.2.2) gross violence is part of the offence charged.

title: Offences against emergency workers, custodial officers and youth justice custodial workers on duty
statement: Protected officials are emergency workers, custodial officers and youth justice custodial workers on duty (including persons employed or engaged by a State, Territory or the Commonwealth to perform similar functions while on duty in Victoria). Minimum non-parole periods: intentionally or recklessly causing serious injury in circumstances of gross violence 5 years; intentionally causing serious injury 3 years; recklessly causing serious injury 2 years; intentionally or recklessly causing injury 6 months. The minimum applies only if it is proved beyond reasonable doubt that a victim was such a worker on duty and that the offender knew or was reckless as to that. It does not apply if: the accused was found guilty on the basis of intentionally directing, assisting or encouraging (on either limb) and proves on the balance of probabilities that their involvement was minor; the offender was under 18 at the time of the offence; or the court finds special reasons. Instead of imprisonment with the minimum, a youth justice centre order of at least the minimum may be made if the offender is under 21 at sentence, the court does not find special reasons, and on a pre-sentence report it believes the offender has reasonable prospects for rehabilitation or is particularly impressionable, immature or likely to be subjected to undesirable influences in an adult prison (not for gross violence charges). If special reasons are found on a charge of intentionally or recklessly causing serious injury or injury (ss 16–18; for ss 15A/15B against a protected official: flag.gross_violence_protected_special_reason), the court must impose imprisonment (without a CCO) or make a mandatory treatment and monitoring order, Residential Treatment Order or Court Secure Treatment Order (whether imprisonment combined with a mandatory treatment and monitoring order is open is unresolved: flag.mtmo_combination_sentence); a therapeutic order only if the offender proves on the balance of probabilities impaired mental functioning at the offence, causally linked to it and substantially and materially reducing culpability, not caused substantially by self-induced intoxication, and the court has received and had regard to a psychiatrist’s or registered psychologist’s report and is satisfied the order is appropriate. The Manual gives no commencement date for these minimums.

title: 'Special reason' to depart from a mandatory minimum
statement: Victorian mandatory minimum provisions provide an exception where the court finds a special reason: it may then decline to impose imprisonment (Category 1 offence) or impose a non-parole period below the minimum. A special reason may exist in four circumstances: (1) the offender assisted or undertook to assist authorities in the prosecution or investigation of an offence; (2) the offender proves on the balance of probabilities a mental impairment at the time of offending, causally related to it, that substantially and materially reduces culpability (not where caused substantially by self-induced intoxication), or that would cause substantially greater than ordinary burdens or risks of imprisonment; (3) the court intends to impose a Court Secure Treatment Order or Residential Treatment Order; (4) substantial and compelling reasons, exceptional and rare, justify not imposing imprisonment — for which the court must regard general deterrence and denunciation as primary, give less weight to personal circumstances than to the nature and gravity of the offending, not consider prior good character (other than a lack of previous convictions or findings of guilt), early plea, rehabilitation prospects or parity, and have regard to Parliament’s intention that a custodial term should ordinarily be imposed. The offender carries the burden, which is heavy and not lightly discharged. The reason must be stated in writing and recorded. For the protected-official injury offences (ss 16–18) and the protected-worker driving offences, a special reason confines the disposition to imprisonment (no CCO) or a therapeutic order (s 5(2GA): cat1.custodial_required; whether imprisonment combined with a mandatory treatment and monitoring order is open is unresolved: flag.mtmo_combination_sentence); for ss 15A/15B against a protected official the disposition other than imprisonment without a CCO is unresolved (flag.gross_violence_protected_special_reason).

title: Standard sentence scheme: when it applies
statement: An offence is a standard sentence offence if the Act creating it or prescribing its maximum specifies a period as the standard sentence. The scheme became effective on 1 February 2018 and applies only to offences committed after that date; it does not apply to offenders under 18 at the time of offending, or to offences heard and determined summarily. Conspiring, inciting or attempting to commit a standard sentence offence is not itself a standard sentence offence. title: Standard sentence: a guidepost, not a starting point
statement: The standard sentence is the sentence for an offence in the middle of the range of seriousness, taking into account only the objective factors (the nature of the offence, not the offender’s personal circumstances; the scheme does not exclude mitigating factors from sentencing). The key requirement is that the court take it into account as a relevant sentencing factor: a legislative guidepost like the maximum, which must not be given too much weight; it does not permit two-stage sentencing, and the court does not start from it and work up or down. Seriousness is assessed as it always has been, as part of the instinctive synthesis. The notional mid-range can be very difficult to identify for offences covering a wide range of conduct (e.g. sexual penetration of a child under 12). Only sentences imposed under the scheme may be used as current sentencing practices (principles from earlier cases remain usable); a sentence that exceeds pre-scheme practice is not for that reason manifestly excessive.

title: Serious offenders (arson, drug, sexual, violent)
statement: When the Supreme or County Court imprisons a 'serious offender' for a 'relevant offence': (1) protection of the community is the principal purpose (the other purposes are not excluded; its weight depends on the assessed risk of re-offending, which the court must assess), and a sentence longer than proportionate may be imposed — rarely, and with reasons for assessing a continuing risk; such a sentence generally widens the gap between head sentence and non-parole period; (2) terms for relevant offending are served cumulatively on any uncompleted sentence unless the court directs otherwise (a prima facie rule: good reason, but not exceptional circumstances, is needed for concurrency; totality still applies); (3) the status is recorded. Serious offenders: serious arson offender (a serious arson offence); serious drug offender (a drug offence); serious sexual offender (two or more sexual offences; persistent sexual abuse of a child under 16; the incidents of a sexual offence in a course of conduct charge; or at least one sexual and one violent offence from the same course of conduct); serious violent offender (a serious violent offence). Relevant offences: arson / drug / sexual or violent / serious violent offence respectively. Each qualifying conviction (in the current hearing or earlier) must have resulted in imprisonment or youth justice centre detention, and must be proved beyond reasonable doubt; Commonwealth, interstate or overseas convictions count if substantially similar and resulting in imprisonment or detention. The status is acquired only after sentence for a qualifying offence, and no serious offender may be a young offender (under 21 when committing the relevant offence). The provisions apply only to relevant offences (not other charges on the indictment) and not to Commonwealth offences. There is no particular relationship with the indefinite sentence scheme. The offence chapters list the qualifying offences: for drug offences, the State offences listed in 28.7 (trafficking or cultivating a large commercial or commercial quantity, and conspiracy, incitement, aiding or abetting, or a preparatory act for them); certain Commonwealth import/export and possession convictions can qualify an offender found guilty of a Victorian Schedule 1 drug offence (28.7: guide.drugs.statutory_schemes); for arson, the listed arson offences (27.5.1: guide.property.statutory_schemes).

title: Failure to fix a non-parole period: correction on application vs appeal
statement: Failure to fix a non-parole period does not invalidate the sentence, and a reviewing court may correct such a failure on application — but only for sentencing irregularities. A deliberate decision not to fix one is within the court’s discretion and is not a basis for a reviewing court to fix one; the remedy is an application for leave to appeal.

title: Total effective sentence, the base sentence, and cumulation across several indictments
statement: When imprisoning for more than one offence the court must generally fix a total effective sentence, usually by individual sentences and orders for cumulation or concurrency. A Victorian judge must select a base sentence, usually the longest individual sentence: using a shorter one risks distorting the process (e.g. undeserved primacy to a lesser offence). With several indictments in one proceeding, the court may cumulate directly towards the total, or cumulate to notional totals for each indictment and then between them; both are correct, the second being more appropriate where each indictment addresses discrete offending.

refs.q: In sentencing an offender to be imprisoned for more than one offence the court must generally fix a total effective sentence. In State sentencing this is usually achieved by imposing individual sentences for each offence and then making orders for concurrency or cumulation of all or part of those sentences.

refs.q: A judge should usually select the longest individual sentence to be the base sentence. Otherwise, there is a risk of distorting the sentencing process if a shorter sentence is used as the ‘base sentence’, it may for example give undeserved primacy to a lesser offence.

refs.q: When an offender is sentenced on multiple indictments in the one proceeding, there are two distinct methods available for cumulation. The first approach is to disregard the different sources of the charges and cumulate directly towards the total effective sentence.

refs.q: The second approach is to cumulate towards notional total sentences for each indictment and then make further orders in respect of those subtotals to reach the final total effective sentence. Both approaches are correct. title: Renzella discretion: the Act is not exclusive; immigration detention; “dead time”; overlap with totality
statement: Section 18 is not the exclusive measure of how pre-sentence detention may be considered. The weight of immigration detention depends on the burden it imposed. “Dead time” is not defined; the Court of Appeal describes it as custody that, with hindsight, should not have been served. In some cases there is no practical difference between the Renzella discretion and totality, both being concerned with fairness and a just sentence.

title: Indefinite sentence review: applications, reports, disputes, presence and appeal standard
statement: On an offender’s review application the court must give the DPP a copy, make directions within 10 working days and hear it within 25 working days. A different judge may review, and may order reports about the period since sentence or last review; reports go to the parties, who may file their own and must exchange them. A disputed report (or part) cannot be considered until the parties may lead evidence and cross-examine its author. On review the parties may lead admissible evidence and make submissions. The offender must be present unless their conduct makes it impracticable (or absence will not prejudice them and is in the interests of justice). On appeal the Court of Appeal may confirm, or set aside and make the proper order; it is an appeal in the strict sense requiring House v The King error.

title: Mandatory minimum non-parole periods: the five groups (plus Serious Offenders Act supervision order breaches)
statement: Beyond Category 1 and 2 imprisonment requirements, for some offences (subject to requirements and exclusions) the court must impose imprisonment with a minimum non-parole period: manslaughter offences; gross violence offences; offences against protected officials; driving offences against protected officials; aggravated home invasion or carjacking. There is also a mandatory minimum term for certain supervision order breaches under the Serious Offenders Act 2018. The intake must screen for each group.

title: Federal offences: a different regime (the app is limited to Victorian offences)
statement: If any charge is a Commonwealth offence, Victorian rules do not simply apply: cumulation is effected by commencement dates and State sentences cannot be cumulated on Commonwealth ones; certain federal offences carry a minimum non-parole period of three-quarters of the head sentence; Boulton does not apply, and s 44 does not apply to federal offenders (so no combination sentence for a single federal offence); mixed indictments need separate, consistent sentences. title: Offender already serving a Commonwealth sentence: direct when the Victorian term commences (s 16(4))
statement: If an offender is already serving a sentence for a Commonwealth offence, the court must direct when the new term commences: no later than immediately after completion of the Commonwealth sentence if no non-parole or pre-release period was fixed, or immediately after the end of any non-parole or pre-release period fixed as part of the Commonwealth sentence. A State sentence cannot be cumulated on a Commonwealth sentence by a cumulation order.
